overview.title: 📖 Overview: Setting Processes in Motion Before Shabbat
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 18a–18b
overview.hebrewSource: וְשָׁוִין אֵלּוּ וְאֵלּוּ, שֶׁטּוֹעֲנִין קוֹרַת בֵּית הַבַּד וְעִגּוּלֵי הַגַּת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The mishna records Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's report that his family gave white clothes to a gentile launderer no fewer than three days before Shabbat, and that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that one may load the olive press and the wine press before Shabbat so the oil and wine keep flowing in on Shabbat itself. The Gemara first traces the underlying dispute about when kneading becomes 'kneading,' then surveys a Tosefta's list of processes people may start before Shabbat and let run on their own — irrigation, incense, sulfur, salve — contrasted with the water mill, which may not be started because of the noise it makes, or because Jewish-owned utensils must themselves 'rest.' That principle of shevitat kelim, traced to Beit Shammai, is then tested against case after case: sulfur under silverware, tubs, lamps, pots on the fire, animal traps. The daf closes by turning to how much advance notice a gentile needs before Shabbat to sell him something, lend him something, or send him on an errand.

slides.title: 👔 The Mishna: Two Customs of Advance Preparation
slides.subtitle: Loading presses and laundering clothes before Shabbat begins
rows: White clothes to a gentile launderer
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's family practice
Given no fewer than three days before Shabbat, since white clothes are hardest to launder
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree: permitted
Set up before Shabbat so oil keeps being squeezed out through Shabbat
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree: permitted
Same principle — the grapes keep yielding wine on their own

callout.label: Why these two agree:
callout.text: Later the Gemara explains: Beit Shammai only decreed against actions that would make one liable to a sin-offering if done on Shabbat itself. Squeezing oil or wine this way carries no such liability, so there was no reason to forbid starting it before Shabbat.

slides.title: 🍞 When Does Kneading Begin?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi vs. Rabbi Yosei on flour, ashes, and ink

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: One person adds the flour, another adds the water into the vessel. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the second person is liable for kneading, even though he never actually kneaded it.

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: Not liable until he actually kneads the dough. Merely wetting it isn't enough.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Maybe Rabbi Yosei only says that about flour, which can be kneaded — but ink can't be kneaded, so maybe wetting alone counts as the full act there?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: No — a parallel baraita about ashes (which also can't be kneaded) has Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda saying the same thing: not liable until actually kneaded.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But were the two baraitot taught together? If not, maybe 'ashes' there really meant kneadable soil.

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Since they weren't taught side by side, that reading can't be proven — but Rav Yosef holds this baraita about ink follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: adding water alone is enough to be liable.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: The mishna's rule that adding water to dry ink powder already counts as 'soaking it' follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position on kneading.

slides.title: 💧 Set It and Let It Run — Except the Mill
slides.subtitle: A Tosefta's list of Friday actions that continue automatically through Shabbat

nodes.content: 📜 Tosefta: before Shabbat one may open a canal to fill a garden all day, place incense under clothes, sulfur under vessels, salve on an eye, a bandage on a wound — all continue 'on their own'
🚫 EXCEPTION: wheat may not be placed in a water mill unless it will finish grinding while it is still day

columns.label: Rabba
columns.content: Forbidden because the mill makes noise — it looks like Shabbat is being desecrated

columns.label: Rav Yosef
columns.content: Forbidden because of shevitat kelim — a Jew's utensils must also 'rest' on Shabbat (Exodus 23:13)

nodes.content: ✅ Rav Yosef's reason is adopted: the obligation for utensils to rest, not mere noise

callout.label: Why this matters:
callout.text: Once 'resting of utensils' is the accepted reason, the Gemara must explain why incense, sulfur, and animal traps — which also keep 'working' through Shabbat — are nevertheless permitted.

slides.title: ⚖️ Testing Beit Shammai's Rule Case by Case
slides.subtitle: If utensils must rest by Torah law (Beit Shammai), why are some active utensils allowed?

boxes.title: No Action Performed
items: Incense/sulfur: permitted because placed on the ground, not held in a vessel obligated to rest
Flax bundles drying in an oven: the oven 'sits idle,' the drying happens on its own
Fish/bird/animal traps: permitted only when they are passive hooks and nets — a trap that actively works is forbidden

boxes.title: Declared Ownerless (Hefker)
items: Fermenting tub, Shabbat lamp, cooking pot, roasting spit — all continue their process into Shabbat
Beit Shammai permits these only if the owner declares them hefker while it is still day
Once ownerless, they are no longer a Jew's utensils obligated to rest

callout.label: Underlying dispute:
callout.text: Rav Oshaya cited Rav Asi: shevitat kelim by Torah law is Beit Shammai's position, not Beit Hillel's. For Beit Hillel, even a utensil that performs a genuine action may be left running.

slides.title: 🕊️ How Much Notice a Gentile Needs Before Shabbat
slides.subtitle: Selling, lending, or handing something to a gentile so he doesn't work for you on Shabbat

steps.content: 1️⃣ Beit Shammai: give it to him only if there's time for him to reach his own house before dark
2️⃣ Beit Hillel: sufficient if there's time to reach a house adjacent to the town wall — a shorter distance
3️⃣ Rabbi Akiva: sufficient if there's time merely to exit the Jew's own doorway — what the gentile does afterward doesn't matter
4️⃣ Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda: Rabbi Akiva isn't a fourth opinion — he is simply explaining what Beit Hillel really meant

callout.label: Same clock, different mitzva:
callout.text: A parallel dispute applies to selling leavened bread (chametz) to a gentile before Passover: Beit Shammai require certainty it will be used up before Passover; Beit Hillel permit selling as long as the Jew himself could still eat it.

summary.principle: Processes that will keep running through Shabbat on their own may be started beforehand, but a Jew's own utensils must not actively 'work' on Shabbat — and dealings with a gentile must be timed so he does not visibly labor for the Jew once Shabbat begins.

flowSteps.content: 👔 Mishna: white clothes to launderer 3 days ahead; press beams loaded before Shabbat by agreement of both houses
🍞 Gemara traces the mishna's kneading assumption to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: adding water alone can complete the prohibited act

columns.content: 💧 Irrigation, incense, sulfur, salve: run 'on their own' — permitted
⚙️ Water mill: forbidden — shevitat kelim, utensils must rest

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Beit Shammai's Torah-level rule tested: hefker or passive placement unlocks each exception
🎓 Key Principle: what may run untended through Shabbat, and how far in advance a gentile must be engaged, both turn on avoiding the appearance — or reality — of labor on Shabbat itself

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what do Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree is permitted before Shabbat?
o: Grinding wheat in a water mill
Loading the beams of the olive press and the wine press
Kneading dough with water added by a second person
Lighting incense under clothing
quiz.e: The mishna states that both houses agree one may load the olive-press beam and the wine press before Shabbat so the oil and wine continue to be produced through Shabbat.

quiz.q: In the baraita about ink, whose opinion does Rav Yosef say underlies the ruling that adding water to dry ink powder already makes one liable?
o: Rabbi Akiva
Rabbi Yosei
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
Rabbi Eliezer
quiz.e: Rav Yosef identifies the mishna's position with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that the last person to add water is liable for kneading even without actually kneading the mixture.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita prohibit placing wheat in a water mill before Shabbat, according to the reason ultimately adopted (Rav Yosef)?
o: Because it makes noise that looks like Shabbat desecration
Because grinding is inherently a Torah-level labor with no exceptions
Because of shevitat kelim — the requirement that a Jew's utensils also rest on Shabbat
Because gentiles are not permitted near the mill
quiz.e: Rav Yosef rejects Rabba's 'noise' explanation in favor of shevitat kelim, derived from Exodus 23:13, which obligates even utensils to rest on Shabbat.

quiz.q: According to Beit Shammai, how could one permissibly leave a cooking pot or Shabbat lamp actively 'working' through Shabbat?
o: By covering it with a cloth
By declaring the utensil ownerless (hefker) before Shabbat begins
By placing it outside the public domain
It could never be left working under any circumstances
quiz.e: Since Beit Shammai holds shevitat kelim applies by Torah law even to utensils performing an actual action, the only way around it is to render the utensil hefker, so it is no longer 'a Jew's utensil.'

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, what is the relationship between Rabbi Akiva's statement and Beit Hillel's opinion about giving an object to a gentile before Shabbat?
o: Rabbi Akiva disagrees sharply with Beit Hillel
Rabbi Akiva is simply explaining what Beit Hillel actually meant
Rabbi Akiva follows Beit Shammai instead
Rabbi Akiva applies only to chametz before Passover
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda states that Rabbi Akiva's ruling — sufficient time to exit the Jew's own doorway — is not a separate position but the true meaning of Beit Hillel's statement.
